title: The Uniqueness of the Resurrection Claim
short: the uniqueness of the resurrection claim

keyTerms.d: The early Christian assertion that Jesus of Nazareth rose bodily from the dead is historically sui generis — it cannot be neatly reduced to its Jewish background, to pagan myth, or to ancient stories of heroes whisked up to heaven. Establishing this does not, by itself, prove the claim true.

Death is real; some interim state follows; and then — only then — comes a return to embodied life. The Greek word translated “raised,” egēgertai, in its Jewish setting meant the reanimation and transformation of a corpse. This is not a ghost and not a metaphor.

When ancient Jews spoke of resurrection they meant something bodily, collective, and future: it would happen to all the righteous together, at the end of the age, as part of God’s restoration of the world. Nobody expected one person to rise ahead of everyone else.

keyTerms.t: A radical modification, not an abandonment
keyTerms.d: The first Christians did not abandon the Jewish hope; they radically modified it. They claimed that the resurrection of the dead — an event everyone agreed was reserved for the last day — had happened to one man, in advance, in the middle of history. The mutation is so specific, and so unmotivated by prior expectation, that it cries out for explanation.

Three things the sources distinguish: escape (Elijah taken, never died), resuscitation (Lazarus, returned to mortal life, died again), and resurrection (raised to immortal, glorified bodily life — the end-time event). The first two existed; the claim about Jesus is the third.

A hero removed from earth and deified is translation, the same pattern as Enoch or Elijah, not resurrection: no empty tomb is at issue because there was no body to begin with. These differ from resurrection in kind, not merely degree.

The three ways the pagan parallels fail on the specifics. Where the parallel sounds closest it is late; where the figure is genuinely old the “rising” is loose — a seasonal alternation of a god in mythic time; and where the story is both old and vivid it is unlike — the god does not come back to this world at all.

The scholarly habit of treating superficial similarity as genetic dependence. A death and a return are not a resurrection unless the specific contours match, and they do not; the burden is to show borrowing rather than coincidence.

derive.q: Jewish hope expected all the righteous raised together at the end of the age; the first Christians proclaimed one man raised, in advance, in the middle of history — so the claim is…?
derive.ans: a radical modification of Jewish hope, not its predictable product
derive.why: The first Christians did not abandon the Jewish hope; they radically modified it. Nobody expected one person to rise ahead of everyone else. The mutation is so specific, and so unmotivated by prior expectation, that it cries out for explanation.

derive.q: Every text that has Adonis raised from the dead, and the only texts that even hint at a rebirth of Attis, were written after Christianity began, largely by Christian writers — so as sources for Easter they are…?
derive.why: Where the parallel sounds closest — Adonis and Attis — it is late: the rising is attested only after Christianity was already being preached, and largely by Christian writers. If the cult did grow a rising of its own in the third and fourth centuries, Jonathan Z. Smith allows, it may have been “in imitation of the Christian myth.”

derive.q: Dumuzi is far older than Christianity, but his “rising” is a half-year below while his sister takes his place for the other half — so the parallel is…?
derive.ans: loose: a seasonal alternation, not a man leaving a grave
derive.why: Honesty requires saying that the dating argument does not dispose of this one. But Jonathan Z. Smith reads this as the opposite of triumph over death: “The myth emphasizes the inalterable power of the realm of the dead, not triumph over it.” The same holds for Baal and Melqart, Mettinger’s other firm cases: their descent and return are tied, on his own account, to the seasons and belong to gods in mythic time, not to a man in a known year.

derive.q: Osiris is murdered, dismembered, reassembled — and then journeys to the underworld to become lord of the dead — so the story is…?
derive.ans: unlike: the god does not come back to this world
derive.why: Here the story is early, but the event is different in kind. He is revived only to rule the underworld, not restored to earthly life. The Osiris story gives the realm of the dead its king; the Easter proclamation is that Christ came back out of that realm, bodily.

derive.q: Romulus vanishes in a sudden storm and is later seen declaring he has become a god; no body, no grave — so the pattern is…?
derive.why: Romulus does not die and return in his body; he is removed from earth, and no empty tomb is at issue because there was no body to begin with — the storm simply takes him. Pagan antiquity had plenty of room for souls surviving and heroes divinized, and precisely because it had those categories it had no need to invent resurrection.

derive.q: Grant all of it: the claim was unprecedented. Does that, by itself, prove it true?
derive.ans: no — uniqueness is not truth; it forces the question where the idea came from
derive.why: That an idea is unprecedented does not make it correct; novel false beliefs arise all the time. The argument clears away the borrowing explanation; the positive case rests on the early creed, the appearances, and the empty tomb, argued separately.

honestState.p1: On the comparative side, the consensus has shifted decisively away from Frazer: following the standard reference treatment, the simple “dying-and-rising god as source of Christianity” thesis is now widely abandoned, while Mettinger, arguing against the prevailing view, has maintained that some such figures genuinely existed. On the Jewish side, Wright’s account of resurrection as bodily, collective, and future is widely accepted even by those who reject his conclusions. What remains contested is not whether the resurrection claim is unusual — that is broadly granted — but what best explains its origin.
honestState.fairness: Mettinger’s finding is an important concession and the question is not closed: Mettinger concluded that some genuine dying-and-rising figures did exist in pre-Christian times — though Mettinger reached that verdict against the prevailing view, and he denied that any of them explains the Christian belief. Mark S. Smith’s 1998 “obituary” for the category is one Mettinger contests for the category itself, but not for the borrowing thesis. The direction-of-influence argument (Bowersock on the Greek novels) is a specific, debated thesis, not a consensus, and the reading of Philostratus as a pagan rejoinder is likewise debated. And critics such as James G. Crossley argue that Wright overstates the historical security of the empty tomb — a genuinely contested claim, and the more disputed half of the case.
honestState.verdict: Uniqueness is not truth. What the argument establishes is narrower but still significant: the resurrection claim cannot be explained away as the predictable product of its Jewish environment, nor as a Jewish edition of a pagan myth, nor as one more tale of a hero taken up to the gods — and the strongest witnesses against those reductions are not friends of Christian apologetics. It clears away the borrowing explanation; the positive case rests on the early creed, the appearances, and the empty tomb, and the most natural explanation of those facts together, for anyone not antecedently committed to ruling miracles out, is that Jesus rose from the dead.

order: If the resurrection story were borrowed or evolved, it should be the predictable product of its supposed sources.
It is not: the first Christians radically modified the Jewish hope, and the pagan parallels are mythic and timeless, not historical and datable.
Therefore the resurrection claim cannot be explained away as a predictable borrowing.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision limit.
cards.a: If the resurrection story were borrowed or evolved, it should be the predictable product of its supposed sources — pagan dying-rising myths or Jewish resurrection hope. Precision: uniqueness is not truth; the claim is only that it cannot be explained away as the predictable product of those sources.

The first Christians did not abandon the Jewish hope; they radically modified it — the resurrection everyone reserved for the last day had happened to one man, in advance. And the pagan parallels are gods bound to the seasonal cycle, mythic and timeless, not historical and datable.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the resurrection claim cannot be explained away as the predictable product of its Jewish environment, nor as a Jewish edition of a pagan myth, nor as one more tale of a hero taken up to the gods. It does not prove the claim true: novel false beliefs arise all the time. It leaves the right question — where did such a strange idea come from?

cards.q: Why does Jewish expectation fail to explain the claim?
cards.a: Resurrection meant something bodily, collective, and future — all the righteous together, at the end of the age. There was no slot for a single man passing through death into deathless, transformed life ahead of everyone else, in the middle of ordinary history.

Escape: taken, never died (Elijah). Resuscitation: returned to mortal life and died again (Lazarus). Resurrection: raised to immortal, glorified bodily life — the end-time event. The first two existed; the claim about Jesus is the third, arrived early for one man.

cards.q: What two questions does the pagan parallel never ask?
cards.a: When is each rising first attested, and what, exactly, rises? Asked of each figure in turn, the parallels come out late, loose, or unlike a bodily resurrection in history.

cards.q: The three ways the parallels fail — state each with its test.
cards.a: Late: where the parallel sounds closest, the rising is attested only after Christianity was already being preached, largely by Christian writers. Loose: where the figure is genuinely old, the “rising” is a seasonal alternation of a god in mythic time. Unlike: where the story is old and vivid, the god does not come back to this world at all but reigns over the dead.

cards.q: One modern study concluded, against what remains the prevailing view, that some genuine dying-and-rising figures existed before Christianity. What does that concession grant — and not grant?
cards.a: It grants that some ancient gods were believed to die and return — a verdict reached against the prevailing view, and one we should not pretend away. It does not grant that any of them is the source of Easter, which is precisely what the scholar who found them denied: the faith in Jesus’ death and resurrection “retains its unique character in the history of religions.”

cards.q: Reply to: Christianity assembled its claim from fragments in an atmosphere of syncretism.
cards.a: Twofold. The mythicist case leans on the very scholar who explicitly denied the materials were used this way. And a death and a return are not a resurrection unless the specific contours match — they do not. The environment was syncretistic, and that much is accurate; the burden is to show borrowing rather than coincidence, and it remains unmet.

cards.q: Reply to: the Gospels are myth deliberately cast as history.
cards.a: The question is origin, not genre — and the earliest evidence is not the Gospels. The claim is already a fixed formula in the creed Paul received, dated by most scholars to within a few years of the crucifixion, with named witnesses still alive to be asked. Ancient writers could dress myth as history; that does not show it happened here, and the date of the earliest testimony tells against it.

cards.q: Reply to: grief and guilt produced a chain reaction of visions.
cards.a: Grief hallucinations are private and individual, ill-suited to the multiple, group, and hostile appearances. The chain reaction presupposes a category for a risen-yet-individual messiah — the very thing the disciples lacked. The least weak of the naturalistic reconstructions, but not the best explanation of the full set of data.

cards.q: Tammuz is genuinely old. Why is he still an unlikely source for Jewish preachers of Easter?
cards.a: His “rising” is a seasonal alternation; the myth emphasizes “the inalterable power of the realm of the dead, not triumph over it.” And to a Jew the Tammuz rite was not raw material but a scandal: Ezekiel is shown the women weeping for Tammuz as one of the “abominations” at the LORD’s own house (Ezekiel 8:13–15).

obj.q: Horus, Mithras, Osiris — born of virgins, dead three days, risen. Christianity is mythology with a Jewish accent.
obj.model: Concede what should be conceded: Mettinger, against what remains the prevailing view, concluded that some genuine dying-and-rising figures did exist in pre-Christian times — Dumuzi, Baal and Melqart, with Adonis and Eshmun as probable further cases. On his finding the category is not empty — a verdict reached against the prevailing view — and we should not pretend it away. What fails is the derivation. The popular list dissolves on inspection: Horus is not born of a virgin nor raised; Roman Mithras is born from a rock and never dies; Osiris is reassembled to rule the dead, not returned to life. These lists trace to 19th-century compilations and internet documentaries, not to the texts — which is why, after Jonathan Z. Smith’s 1987 treatment, the simple dying-and-rising-god derivation is now widely abandoned. And Mettinger’s own verdict: the faith in the death and resurrection of Jesus “retains its unique character in the history of religions.”

obj.q: Even the most careful scholar grants some dying-and-rising gods were real. Ezekiel saw women weeping for Tammuz at the temple gate; Adonis’s image was brought out “as if alive”; the Day of Blood sat beside a Day of Joy for Attis. Death, lament, third-day rejoicing — it was on the first Christians’ doorstep.
obj.model: The answer turns on two questions the parallel never asks: when is each rising first attested, and what, exactly, rises? Every text that has Adonis raised from the dead was written after the gospel was already being preached; the only texts that hint at a rebirth of Attis are two late, post-Christian reflections, and Attis is not among the figures even Mettinger accepts. Where the figure is genuinely old — Dumuzi, Baal, Melqart — the “rising” is a seasonal alternation of a god in mythic time, not a man leaving a grave; and Osiris does not come back to this world at all but reigns over the dead. None of this denies Mettinger’s finding that some ancient gods were believed to die and return; it denies that any of them is the source of Easter, which is precisely what Mettinger himself denied. The objection does not hold.

obj.q: No single pagan story has to match. Christianity assembled its claim from fragments — a death here, a return there, a meal from the mysteries — and Mettinger’s own concessions show the raw materials were available. And the very datedness of Jesus’ story is just the Jewish historicizing contribution.
obj.model: The reply is twofold. First, Carrier leans on Mettinger while Mettinger himself explicitly denied that the materials were used this way — a tension Bart Ehrman, himself an agnostic New Testament scholar, has pressed, noting that the relevant evidence is ambiguous and does not bear the weight mythicism places on it. Second, the charge of “parallelomania” — treating superficial similarity as genetic dependence — applies with full force: a death and a return are not a resurrection unless the specific contours match, and they do not. The environment was syncretistic, and that much is accurate; the burden, though, is to show borrowing rather than coincidence, and that burden remains unmet. And the borrowing thesis still has to explain what no parallel supplies: why Jewish monotheists, whose prophets counted weeping for Tammuz an abomination, proclaimed that the God of Israel had raised a crucified man bodily, once, within living memory, as the firstfruits of the resurrection they expected at the end of the age.

obj.q: I’ll grant they were sincere. Peter, wracked by grief and guilt, had a vision, and it set off a chain reaction. Paul’s was a conversion vision, James’s a reconciliation vision — no one mechanism needs to cover them all.
obj.model: This account at least takes the disciples’ sincerity seriously rather than alleging fraud. But grief hallucinations are private and individual, ill-suited to explain the multiple, group, and even hostile appearances (Paul, James) reported in 1 Corinthians 15. And the framework presupposes that the disciples already held a category into which a risen-yet-individual messiah could fit — the very thing Wright shows they lacked. Even granting that Paul and James can be handled one at a time, Wright’s missing-category point still blocks the “chain reaction”: a community with no slot for a single man risen ahead of the last day is an odd seedbed for visions of exactly that; and the bodily, tangible phenomenology the sources report — eating, being touched — together with the empty tomb resists a clean visionary reduction. Of the naturalistic reconstructions, the visionary theory is the least weak — but it still does not account for the group and hostile appearances, nor supply the missing category; it is not the best explanation of the full set of data.

unseen.q: Apollonius of Tyana was a first-century wonder-worker who disappeared into heaven. A miracle-working sage with a heavenly exit — the Jesus story looks like one more of those.
unseen.model: The Apollonius case is weaker even than Romulus’s on its own terms. His biography by Philostratus was written more than a century after his death, and by Philostratus’s own admission the memoir of his companion Damis — his principal source, and the only one written by a professed eyewitness — breaks off before Apollonius dies, so neither his death nor any assumption into heaven is recorded by the one witness who could have reported it; Philostratus falls back on frankly contradictory “stories” about his end, one of which has him vanish into a temple whose doors close behind him. Nor is the resemblance likely to run the way a borrowing thesis needs: some scholars have read the Life as, in part, a pagan rejoinder to the Gospel story rather than an independent source lying behind it — a debated thesis, not a settled fact, but enough to show the parallel cannot simply be assumed to run from Apollonius to Jesus. And a heavenly disappearance is translation, not resurrection — a difference in kind, not merely degree. By contrast, the resurrection claim is already a fixed formula in the creed Paul received, dated by most scholars to within a few years of the crucifixion, with named witnesses still alive to be asked. That clears away the borrowing explanation; it does not by itself prove the resurrection, whose positive case rests on the early creed, the appearances, and the empty tomb.
